### Thanksgiving Closes With the Storm's Count at 961,000 Dark and the Parade Waiting for Saturday, Brent Holding at $96.19 in the Early Friday Trade After Its $96.57 Settlement, Asia Higher at Its Open With the Kospi Up 2.2 Percent, Europe's Next Central Bank President Named in Brussels, and No Word From Moscow on the Merkury Into a Sixth Day

Filed as: Edition No. 96 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-27T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-27-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Thanksgiving Closes With the Storm’s Count at 961,000 Dark and the Parade Waiting for Saturday, Brent Holding at $96.19 in the Early Friday Trade After Its $96.57 Settlement, Asia Higher at Its Open With the Kospi Up 2.2 Percent, Europe’s Next Central Bank President Named in Brussels, and No Word From Moscow on the Merkury Into a Sixth Day

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a holiday spent in the dark in four states; an oil price that held its gain into Friday; a rally made abroad, waiting for its first American test; a presidency settled in Brussels for February; and the same three silences—a refinery’s owner, a strait’s hulls, and a ministry—carried over the turn of the log.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Friday, November 27, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 95, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Thursday, in Edition No. 94, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Thursday, in Edition No. 93, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Thursday, and in Edition No. 92, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Thursday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Thanksgiving Settled, What It Left Open

Thanksgiving settled its storm count, its European closes, its oil settlement, and one presidency in Brussels—and left Friday’s half session, Sunday’s producers’ meeting, and three standing silences to the next day of the log. The storm’s last full count stands at more than 961,000 customers without power at 1930 Eastern, in the wire’s evening account filed below, with 440 flights cancelled and more than 2,200 delayed. Brent settled at $96.57 and held at $96.19 in the first Friday trade. Asia opened its Friday higher in two of the three morning readings filed below. In Brussels, the euro area’s leaders put forward Mr. Hern&aacute;ndez de Cos to take the European Central Bank in February. In the strait, Thursday closed at two crossings. In Ukraine, the day added two more dead to the night’s two. Off Benghazi, the eastern army named its dead officers and promised an answer.

What Thanksgiving settled is the storm’s peak counts, as counts; Europe’s closes, on a day with no American session to answer them; Brent’s settlement, the highest since November 6; the succession at the European Central Bank, subject to the December formalities; and Thursday’s crossing count, at two. What it left open is the restoration clock in Virginia and Pennsylvania; Friday’s shortened session, the first American test of a rally made entirely abroad; the producers’ meeting on Sunday; the state of Ras Tanura, undescribed by its owner into a third day; the two tankers off Khasab, unnamed for a day and a night; the strike Kyiv says Moscow is preparing; and the Russian defence ministry’s account of its corvette, unissued into a sixth day.

Thanksgiving at Midnight: 961,000 Dark at 1930, and the Storm Departing Into New England

The storm closed the holiday as it had spent it, and the evening’s counts are the day’s settled figures. More than 961,000 utility customers had no power at 1930 Eastern—more than 235,000 in Pennsylvania, over 180,000 in New Jersey, 156,000 in Maryland, 132,000 in Virginia, nearly 106,000 in Missouri, more than 56,000 in New York state and more than 21,000 in Delaware—in the wire account above. The Journal’s early-evening count, in the storm account filed below, stood at more than 730,000 along the East Coast and mid-Atlantic alone, and the Associated Press count, in the holiday account filed below, at more than 900,000 homes and businesses. The three counts are readings of one tracker at three hours, and they rise in the order they were taken. Flights closed the day at 440 cancellations and more than 2,200 delays in the wire’s final count, against 417 and some 1,800 at the Evening Watch’s stamp—the correction is stated here, in the open, as the log requires.

The weather’s own line at the close is departure. Conditions improve gradually across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the heaviest rain and strongest winds move into New England, the Weather Service said, with gusts of 25 to 35 miles an hour still expected on Friday. The flood file stands as the evening printed it: significant inundation in Virginia, the Delaware Bay, the Chesapeake Bay and the southern New Jersey coast, Avalon seeing some of the worst flooding in its history in its administrator’s words, and nearly two million water customers in two Maryland counties asked to conserve water against intermittent power failures. No storm fatality had been confirmed in the coastal accounts by Thursday night, in the travel account filed below, with damage surveys still under way. The 100th Macy’s parade stands where the day put it, postponed to Saturday, the first weather rescheduling in its history. Settled: the peak day and its counts. Open: the restoration—broken poles and trees on lines, in Dominion’s warning, mean days in some areas—and the water still standing in New England at the turn.

The Markets at Midnight: A Rally Made Abroad, Asia Higher at the Open, and Friday’s Half Session the First American Test

Europe’s closes stand where the Evening Watch printed them, and the second tally filed below adds its own figures beside them: the STOXX 600 up about 1.8 percent at 636.98 in the closing accounts, and up 2.04 percent at 638.89 in the closing tally filed below, with Milan up 2.36 percent at 48,362.35 and Stellantis up 8.82 percent. The futures closed the holiday session higher—the S&P 500 futures up 0.54 percent in the evening’s account, and up 0.66 percent at 7,243.50 at 1152 Eastern in the tally—and Friday’s session is set: the exchanges reopen at 0930 and close early at 1300, three and a half hours in which to test a rally that no American cash trade has yet touched.

Asia gave the rally its next reading before the log turned, and the readings do not all point the same way. In the wire’s morning account, in the Asia account filed below, the Kospi rose 2.2 percent to 4,812.65, the Nikkei added 0.7 percent to 57,919.30, Sydney rose 0.4 percent and Hong Kong 0.4 percent, with Shanghai down 0.1 percent. In a second account, in the early-session wrap filed below, every open market rose, the Kospi up 2.72 percent at 4,839.20 and the Nikkei up 1.17 percent at 58,172.04 at Tokyo’s lunch break. In a third, in the opening account filed below, both indexes opened higher and then turned lower, the Kospi down 0.34 percent at 4,695.09 and the Nikkei down 0.04 percent at 57,474.52. The desk prints the three as three readings at three hours of one morning, and takes no one of them as the morning. Settled: Thursday’s closes. Open: Asia’s own close, and Friday in New York.

Frankfurt at Midnight: Mr. Hern&aacute;ndez de Cos Put Forward, and December Still the Rates Question

The day’s one appointment was settled in Brussels. The European Council has put forward Pablo Hern&aacute;ndez de Cos as the next President of the European Central Bank, in the Council’s own release filed below: once confirmed, he replaces Christine Lagarde when she leaves office on February 7, 2027, for a term of eight years, not renewable. The euro area’s member states agreed to recommend him, with Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier for the executive board, the Council’s President, Mr. Costa, said on Thursday, in the wire account filed below, paving the way for the formal appointment in December. Parliament and the governing council are still to be consulted; the accounts treat those steps as formalities, and the desk prints them as steps still standing.

The appointment lands on the desk the October minutes built. The minutes, as the Evening Watch printed them, show a large number of members ready to raise rates in October itself, a unanimous hold at a 2.50 percent deposit rate, and a December increase priced at 91 percent in one account and 93 percent in another; the council meets December 16 and 17 with new staff forecasts. Mr. Hern&aacute;ndez de Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain and the present head of the Bank for International Settlements, takes the chair in February, after the December question is answered by the council he will then lead. Settled: the name, and the date. Open: the consultations, the December formal appointment, and the December meeting that precedes both.

Oil at Midnight: Brent at $96.19 in the Early Trade, and the Producers Meeting on Sunday

Oil held its Thanksgiving gain into Friday’s first trade. Brent fell 38 cents, or 0.39 percent, to $96.19 a barrel by 0140 GMT—2040 Eastern, inside this watch’s collection—after settling at $96.57 on Thursday, its highest close since November 6, in the Friday account above; West Texas stood at $85.41, up $1.73, or 2.07 percent, from Wednesday’s close, there having been no settlement on the holiday. Both benchmarks are headed for their first weekly gain in four weeks. The analysts’ note in the same account puts the next figure in the file plainly: Brent can push above $100 without another major escalation, the ANZ analysts wrote, but it increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply.

The supply file itself did not move at the turn. Jazan stands confirmed in the Saudi energy ministry’s words—a projectile, a Nepalese worker killed, several wounded, some operations halted—and Ras Tanura stands where it has stood since Wednesday: claimed hit by the Houthis, smoke in the satellite pictures, loadings suspended in one source’s account, and no word from the plant’s owner, in any account at the stamp, into a third day. The producers’ ministers meet on Sunday, November 29, and the expectation in the Friday account is that the group maintains its output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027. Settled: the settlement, and the early trade’s hold on it. Open: Sunday’s meeting, and the evidence of constrained supply the $100 figure is said to wait on.

The Strait at Midnight: Two Crossings Close Thursday, 47 in Seven Days, and the Hulls Off Khasab Still Unnamed

Thursday closed in the visible counter at two crossings, both outbound, both tankers, the last of them the Asha at 1040 UTC, and no ship had crossed in the new day as of 0122 UTC on Friday, in the counter’s brief filed below. The seven-day count stands at 47 crossings—29 inbound, 18 outbound, 17 of them tankers—at 6.7 a day, about 8 percent of the pre-crisis rate. The evening’s forms of the same counter carried 48, 50 and 51 for the seven days at their several stamps; the brief’s 47 is the latest reading, and the desk prints the succession here, in the open, rather than smoothing it. The status stands severely restricted, as it has stood since October 19.

Against the two counted crossings stand the Guards’ two tankers off Khasab, claimed on mines in Thursday’s early hours, one a supertanker with more than two million barrels aboard, in the Guards account filed below—unnamed, uncrewed in any account, and unconfirmed by any maritime authority in the day and night that followed. The one confirmed incident in the file remains the British office’s: a projectile explosion close to a tanker 50 nautical miles west of Dubai on Wednesday, crew safe, no damage, in the safety account filed below, which also carries the week’s one institutional answer: eight shipping associations wrote jointly on November 26 calling for concrete measures to safeguard freedom of navigation and protect seafarers. Settled: Thursday’s two, and the letter. Open: the hulls, the crews, and the count’s next day.

Ukraine at Midnight: Two More Dead in the Day’s Strikes, Seven Regions on Schedules, and the Larger Strike Still Said to Be Coming

The night’s file stands as the evening printed it—ballistic missiles and 113 drones, two killed and three injured in Kharkiv, power cut in seven regions—in the operator’s file filed below, with the seven regions named in the outages account filed below: Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Kharkiv and Chernihiv, on hourly schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 stages through the day. The day’s strikes then added to the count in the capitals’ own local words. In Kharkiv an 86-year-old woman was killed when a jet-powered drone struck a university building, the mayor and the governor confirming a further strike on an energy facility in the city; in Sloviansk two guided bombs on residential areas killed a man of 37 and wounded another resident, with more than 25 buildings damaged, in the strikes account filed below.

The grid’s detail from the other side’s trade press is printed with its source on it: substations hit at 330 kV in Kharkiv, at 150 kV in Zeleny Hai in the Dnipropetrovsk region, where the account calls the situation critical, and at 110 kV in Radomyshl in the Zhytomyr region, in the substations account filed below. President Zelensky’s warning stands as he gave it on Thursday: preparations for a new massive strike are nearing completion, energy, logistics and essential services the likely targets, and interceptors for the Patriot and NASAMS systems the key task he named. Moscow’s defence ministry’s own account of its strike stands as the evening printed it. Settled: the day’s dead, in the local counts, and the schedules. Open: the strike said to be coming, on no date given.

Libya at Midnight: The Eastern Army Names Its Officers and Pledges an Answer, and the Ministry Is Silent Into a Sixth Day

Benghazi’s file gained names and a promise on Thursday. The Libyan National Army said its two naval officers died of wounds from Sunday’s strike and pledged to retaliate against Kyiv at a time and place of its choosing, in the reprisal account filed below. The officers are named there: Al-Taher Abdullah al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Mohammed al-Said. At least ten people, Libyan and Russian, were wounded, the force said. An obituary surfaced by a Ukrainian monitoring group identified the corvette’s Russian deputy commander among the dead—a claim the desk prints as it stands, surfaced and unconfirmed. The same account carries the investigation’s first Libyan figures: at least four drones intercepted and two striking the vessel, against the seven Kyiv says it deployed, and a launch base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, against the mothership in Kyiv’s own confirmation of Wednesday.

Italy called the operation a mistake, the account adds, and the eastern government has taken the case to the United Nations Security Council, having already asked for an international investigation. Against all of it, the one word the file has waited for since Sunday stands unissued for another day. The Kremlin’s spokesman said on Monday that any information would come from the Defence Ministry; the ministry has confirmed nothing, denied nothing, and published no account of the Merkury or her crew, and at the midnight stamp that silence enters its sixth calendar day. Settled: the officers’ names, in their own force’s words, and the pledge. Open: the pledge’s execution, the inquiry’s findings, and the ministry’s word.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On the storm’s dark: more than 961,000 customers at 1930 Eastern in the wire’s tracker reading, more than 900,000 in the Associated Press’s evening form, more than 730,000 on the East Coast and mid-Atlantic alone in the Journal’s earlier reading, and 800,000 to 900,000 nationwide in the travel account—four readings of one tracker at four hours, rising and then settling in the order taken. On Asia’s Friday open: the Kospi up 2.2 percent and the Nikkei up 0.7 percent in the wire’s morning account, up 2.72 and 1.17 percent in the early-session wrap, and both lower after opening higher in the opening account—three hours of one morning, not one morning. On the STOXX 600’s close: up about 1.8 percent at 636.98 in the closing accounts, up 2.04 percent at 638.89 in the closing tally. On Brent’s Thursday rise: $1.96 in dollars, 1.2 percent in the settlement account’s own figure, and about 2.1 percent in the arithmetic. On the strait’s seven days: 47 crossings in the counter’s latest brief, against 48, 50 and 51 in its own earlier forms. On the Benghazi drones: seven deployed in Kyiv’s word, four intercepted and two striking in the Libyan officials’ account—six accounted for of seven, on that arithmetic. On the launch: a mothership in Kyiv’s confirmation, a base in western Libya in the Libyan officials’ account. Inside the triangle is where the midnight honestly stands, and the log turns on it. The parade is Saturday; the producers meet Sunday; the Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 20 items.

 
 SubjectiveThe Wall Street Journal — Powerful Storm Hits East Coast, Scrambling Thanksgiving PlansA major storm scrambled Thanksgiving Day plans along the East Coast, with heavy winds and rain causing power outages, flight cancellations and the postponement of Macy’s annual holiday parade. The National Weather Service said widespread coastal flooding was under way along the mid-Atlantic and New England coastline, with significant inundation in Virginia, the Delaware Bay and parts of the Chesapeake Bay and the southern New Jersey coast, and 1 to 3 inches of rain expected with scattered flash flooding possible. About 2,100 flights within, into or out of the United States were delayed and more than 400 canceled, according to FlightAware. As of early Thursday evening, more than 730,000 people were without power along the East Coast and mid-Atlantic, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey each above 100,000, with another 116,000 outages in Missouri after snow; PPL Electric Utilities in Pennsylvania said it had restored power to more than 15,000 people. Wind gusts exceeding 30 miles an hour were recorded across all five New York boroughs, including 56 miles an hour at LaGuardia Airport.

The Weather Service said conditions would gradually improve across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the heaviest rain and strongest winds moved into New England, with blustery conditions and gusts of 25 to 35 miles an hour expected across parts of the East Coast on Friday.

 SubjectiveThe Associated Press, carried by WVLT — Heavy rain, wind and flooding plague much of US on Thanksgiving holidayHoliday storms flooded East Coast communities, knocked out power to nearly a million customers and prompted the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity Thursday evening, the majority in East Coast states, according to PowerOutage.us. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The storms flooded areas from North Carolina through New Jersey as high tide rolled in; Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, its borough administrator said. In Maryland, nearly two million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm.

 SubjectiveThe Traveler — Thanksgiving storm snarls East Coast travel with outages, floodingA Thanksgiving Day storm sweeping from the Mid-Atlantic to New England flooded coastal communities, knocked out electricity to hundreds of thousands of customers and caused widespread travel disruption. By Thursday evening PowerOutage.us reported more than 800,000 to 900,000 customers without electricity nationwide, the majority in East Coast states including Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania, with a separate winter system producing snow and additional outages in the Midwest. FlightAware reported more than 2,000 delays and over 400 cancellations by Thursday evening, affecting hubs including New York, Philadelphia, Washington and Boston; Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor operated with speed restrictions and periodic delays south of New York. The centennial Macy’s parade was rescheduled for Saturday, November 28, the first weather-related postponement in its history, and New York State declared an emergency for parts of the downstate region. No storm-related fatalities had been confirmed in the coastal incidents covered by Thursday night, with damage surveys still under way.

The account records the Saudi energy ministry’s statement that a projectile struck the Jazan refinery on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, and states that OPEC+ is likely to maintain its output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027 at its meeting on Sunday.

 SubjectiveBigGo Finance — Brent Holds Near November Peak as Hormuz Mine Attacks and Saudi Refinery Strikes Keep Supply Fears AliveBrent crude futures traded close to their highest level of the month on Friday, slipping 38 cents, or 0.39 percent, to $96.19 a barrel by 0140 GMT after settling at $96.57 on Thursday, the strongest close since November 6. ### Europe Closes Up 1.8 Percent on the Tariff Caps With New York Dark, the Storm Leaves More Than 836,000 Without Power and the Parade on Saturday, a Second Refinery Is Confirmed Hit at Jazan While Ras Tanura's Owner Still Files No Word, Brent Settles at $96.57, and the ECB's Minutes Point to December

Filed as: Edition No. 95 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-26T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-26-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Europe Closes Up 1.8 Percent on the Tariff Caps With New York Dark, the Storm Leaves More Than 836,000 Without Power and the Parade on Saturday, a Second Refinery Is Confirmed Hit at Jazan While Ras Tanura’s Owner Still Files No Word, Brent Settles at $96.57, and the ECB’s Minutes Point to December

 The evening file—the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side: a rally that closed in Europe untested by New York; a central bank’s minutes that moved December closer; a storm that arrived on the holiday it was forecast for; a second refinery confirmed hit by the ministry that owns it, beside a first whose owner has still not spoken; and a strait that ended the day as it began it, two hulls claimed and two crossings counted.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Thursday, November 26, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 94, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, from Edition No. 93, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 92, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief: A Rally Untested, a Storm Arrived, and a Second Refinery Named

In brief: the day’s developments whole are a European rally that closed at its highs with no American session to test it; a set of central-bank minutes that put a December increase at the centre of the file; a coastal storm that spent Thanksgiving Day doing what its forecast said it would do, and left more than 836,000 customers dark by the late afternoon; and, on the Gulf files, the day’s one new confirmed fact—a projectile struck the refinery at Jazan, in the Saudi energy ministry’s own statement—filed beside the Ras Tanura file, whose central question still has no answer from the plant’s owner. Europe’s close stands in the closing account filed below. The storm’s afternoon counts stand in the wire account filed below. The Jazan statement stands in the Saudi account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the evening settled is Europe’s closes, the minutes’ text, the storm’s counts, Jazan in the ministry’s words, and Brent’s settlement. What it left open is Ras Tanura, in any owner’s words; the two tankers off Khasab, unnamed for a full day; the ministry’s word on the Merkury; and the strike Kyiv says is in preparation.

Europe at the Close: Up 1.8 Percent, Every Sector Higher, and No New York to Answer It

The midday rally held to the bell and added to itself. The Stoxx 600 closed up 1.8 percent at 636.98, in the closing account filed below—1.83 percent in the futures account filed below—with the benchmark indexes of Germany, Spain and Italy each gaining more than 2 percent: the DAX up 2.1 percent at 25,215.52 in one closing account and 2.14 percent in the other, the CAC 40 up 1.6 percent at 8,108.74 against 1.71 percent, the FTSE 100 up 1.77 percent, the IBEX up 2.35 percent and the MIB up more than 2 percent in both. Every major sector finished higher; miners, automakers and defence shares each advanced more than 3 percent; Soitec closed up 7 percent and Infineon up 3.6 percent in the closing account, against 5.2 and 4.4 percent at midday. Imperial Brands rose 13.3 percent on Altria’s statement that it is considering an all-cash offer—17.6 percent in one social account, a figure the desk prints in the Cocked Hat and nowhere else.

The stated reason did not change: the tariff file’s shape—the new duties replace rather than add to the old, and the European rate is capped at the 15 percent of the 2025 agreement. Asia’s closes stand where the Midday Watch corrected them. The American reading is futures only: the S&P 500 futures closed up 38.75 points, or 0.54 percent, with no cash session. Settled: the closes, on two continents. Open: Friday’s shortened session, the first American test of a rally made entirely abroad.

The ECB Minutes: A Large Number Ready in October, a Unanimous Hold, and December Priced Above Ninety Percent

The afternoon’s document is the account of the European Central Bank’s meeting of October 28-29, published Thursday. Its operative lines, in the Dow Jones account filed below, are these: a large number of members said the data since September had confirmed the case for further tightening and that they could have supported raising rates at the October meeting itself; all members supported the hold, on the understanding that the communication would convey that another increase would likely be necessary unless the inflation outlook improved significantly; and waiting to reassess in December was, in the account’s words, a reasonable decision. The deposit rate stands at 2.50 percent, after increases in June and September. The pause’s reasons are stated in the same account: underlying inflation broadly stable, no material second-round effects in wages, and financial conditions already tighter.

The market’s reading moved in one direction. Money markets priced a 91 percent probability of a December increase in the midday briefing the Midday Watch filed, and 93 percent in one afternoon account of the minutes; the euro rose 0.10 percent to about 1.0986. The council meets on December 16-17, with new staff forecasts. Settled: the October council’s mind, in its own account. Open: December 17.

Thanksgiving at Evening: 836,000 Dark at 1606, 417 Flights Cancelled, and the Storm Moving Into New England

The storm spent the day on the coast it was forecast for, and the evening’s file is its counts. More than 836,000 utility customers had no power at 1606 Eastern, in the wire account filed below—more than 174,000 in Virginia, 172,000 in Maryland, almost 170,000 in Pennsylvania, more than 117,000 in Missouri, over 91,000 in New Jersey, more than 20,000 in Delaware and nearly 16,000 in North Carolina. The Journal’s early-afternoon count, in the storm account filed below, stood above 550,000 on the East Coast and mid-Atlantic, with Dominion’s warning that broken poles and trees on lines mean days before restoration in some areas, and 123,000 more out in Missouri under snow. FlightAware counted 417 cancellations and some 1,800 delays by the afternoon, Washington Dulles the hardest-hit airport in the Journal’s account; the morning’s figures, 357 cancellations by 0730, stand corrected here in the open.

The weather itself is in the weather service’s words: gusts of 50 to 70 miles an hour across the mid-Atlantic and coastal New England, 56 miles an hour at LaGuardia, and widespread coastal flooding under way, with significant inundation in Virginia, the Delaware Bay, the Chesapeake Bay and the southern New Jersey coast. The service’s evening line is that the storm departs overnight into Friday, its heaviest rain and strongest winds moving into New England. The 100th Macy’s parade stands postponed to Saturday, the first weather rescheduling in its history. Settled: the day’s counts. Open: the night’s water in New England, and the restoration clock in Virginia.

Saudi at Evening: Jazan Confirmed by the Ministry, Ras Tanura Still the Owner’s Silence, and the Yemen Exchange Counted Both Ways

The Saudi file gained its second confirmed refinery strike on Thursday, from the owner’s side of the table. A projectile struck the refinery in the southwestern Jazan region, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several others, sparking a fire and temporarily suspending some operations, according to the Saudi Ministry of Energy, in the account filed below. The coalition’s Thursday statement, in the Jazan account filed below, attributes the attack to the Houthis. At Ras Tanura the file stands where midday left it: loadings suspended in one source’s statement, smoke in the satellite pictures, four interceptions in the coalition’s—and no word from Aramco, approached again on Thursday, in any account at the stamp.

The exchange across the Red Sea is now counted by both sides, and the desk prints both counts. The coalition said it destroyed 50 targets across Sanaa, Hodeidah and Saada on Thursday. The Houthi side counted 109 Saudi strikes over the previous 24 hours, and its health ministry in Sanaa said at least 19 civilians had been killed and 25 wounded over 48 hours. Neither count is confirmed by the other side. Settled: Jazan, in the ministry’s words, and one worker dead. Open: Ras Tanura, in the owner’s words, into a third day.

Oil: Brent Settles at $96.57, and the Producers Meet on Sunday

Brent settled at $96.57 a barrel, up $1.96, in the settlement account filed below—the wire’s own percentage for the rise is 1.2 percent, and the desk prints the wire’s figure beside the wire’s dollars in the Cocked Hat. West Texas Intermediate did not settle, there being no settlement on the holiday; it stood up $1.16, or 1.39 percent, at $84.84 at 1321 Eastern. The week’s arithmetic is two settlements—$94.61 on Wednesday, $96.57 on Thursday—both made on the Gulf files, not on the inventory figures. The producers’ ministers meet on Sunday, November 29, to set 2027 output policy; two people with knowledge of the matter told the wire the group may roll over its current targets for at least the first quarter of 2027. Settled: the settlement. Open: Sunday’s meeting, with a refinery’s state still undescribed by its owner.

The Strait at Evening: Two Crossings All Day, and Two Hulls Unnamed for a Day

Thursday closed in the visible counter as it stood at midday: two crossings, both outbound, both tankers—the Shen Zhou at 0436 UTC and the Asha at 1040 UTC—in the counter’s evening form filed below, stamped 2118 UTC. No third crossing was counted in the eleven hours after the Asha. Wednesday stands closed at six in the counter, correcting the four the Evening Watch printed on Wednesday from the counter’s own earlier stamp—the correction is stated here, in the open, as the log requires. Against the two counted crossings stand the Guards’ two tankers off Khasab, one a supertanker with more than two million barrels, claimed on mines in the morning and not named, not crewed and not confirmed by any maritime authority in the day that followed. Tehran’s count for the week stands at five vessels claimed on mines; the counter’s, at 48 crossings completed. Settled: Thursday’s two. Open: the five, unnamed.

Ukraine at Evening: Two Dead in Kharkiv, the Hardest-Hit Named, and Interceptors Named as the Key Task

The night’s toll gained its figure in the afternoon: two people killed and three injured in Kharkiv, in the running file filed below, from the ballistic missiles and 113 drones Kyiv counted overnight. The seven dark regions stand as the ministry and the operator stated them, with hourly schedules running to the end of Thursday. The president’s evening account, in the coordination account filed below, names the hardest-hit: Dnipro, its district and Pavlohrad; Odesa and its region; Kharkiv region; Konotop and Sumy region.

Two further claims stand with their labels on. Kyiv’s side reported that Russia targeted two foreign civilian ships carrying more than 100,000 tonnes of grain near Odesa, in the grain-ships account filed below, which states that the claims have not been independently verified. And the president’s warning stands as he gave it: Moscow is finishing preparations for a new massive strike, no date given, and the key task he named is interceptors for the Patriot and NASAMS systems. Moscow’s defence ministry said its forces carried out a massive strike on Kyiv’s military-industrial facilities; on the Merkury it filed no word, into the sixth day since Sunday’s sinking. Settled: the two dead, and the seven regions. Open: the strike said to be coming, and the ministry’s word.

The Cocked Hat

Where the evening bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Brent’s rise: up $1.96 to $96.57 in the settlement account, whose own percentage is 1.2 percent against the 2.1 percent the dollars make. On the DAX’s close: up 2.1 percent at 25,215.52 in one closing account, up 2.14 percent in the futures account’s table, and up 1.72 percent at 25,127.68 in a third account’s intraday reading carried as a close. On Imperial Brands: up 13.3 percent in the closing account, about 17.6 percent in the social account. On Seoul’s and Taipei’s closes: up 0.29 and 2.5 percent in the closing accounts, 1.71 and 3.14 percent in the scoreboard. On the strait’s seven days: 48 crossings in the counter’s news form, 50 in its status form, 51 in its midday form. On the storm’s dark: more than 836,000 customers at 1606 Eastern in the wire’s count, more than 550,000 on the coast alone at the Journal’s earlier stamp. On Yemen: 50 targets destroyed in the coalition’s count, 109 strikes in the Houthi count, and 19 civilians dead in the Sanaa health ministry’s, none confirmed by the other side. Inside the triangle is where the evening honestly stands. The Midnight Watch collects at 0000.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 26 items.

Imperial Brands surged 13.3 per cent after Altria said it was considering a possible all-cash offer. Trading volumes were lighter than usual with Wall Street closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.

 SubjectiveJBizNews — European Stocks Jump as Tariff Fears Ease; STOXX 600 Gains 1.8%, DAX Rises 2.1%The STOXX 600 gained 1.8% to close at 636.98, while Germany’s DAX climbed 2.1% to 25,215.52 and France’s CAC 40 rose 1.6% to 8,108.74. With U.S. exchanges shut Thursday, Wednesday, November 25, remained the latest completed U.S. stock-market session: the Dow Jones Industrial Average finished at 50,182.95, up 164.25 points, or 0.33%, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,182.78, down 18.31 points, or 0.25%.

 SubjectiveinvestingLive — European stocks surge, S&P 500 futures finish higher in Thanksgiving tradingThe US Thanksgiving holiday didn’t stand in the way of a strong day for global equities as European stock markets surged and S&P 500 futures closed up 38.75 points, or 0.54%. US stock and bond markets are closed today for Thanksgiving.

 SubjectiveMorningstar, carrying Dow Jones Newswires — ECB Saw Need for Another Rate Hike Unless Inflation Outlook Improved ‘Significantly’Many officials at the European Central Bank viewed another rise in the key interest rate as necessary unless there was a significant cooling of the outlook for inflation, according to an account of their deliberations in October released Thursday. The ECB’s governing council last month left its key rate unchanged at 2.5%. ‘Communication needed to sustain existing policy rate expectations by conveying that another rate hike would likely be necessary unless the inflation outlook improved significantly,’ members of the council agreed. In September, the ECB’s economists raised their forecast for average inflation in 2027 to 2.5% from 2.3%, further above the 2% target.

 SubjectiveFXStreet — Euro ticks higher as ECB minutes reveal appetite for further tighteningMinutes released on Thursday showed that many ECB policymakers could have backed a rate hike in October after data released since the September meeting strengthened the case for tighter policy. All members ultimately agreed to keep rates unchanged, favouring a measured approach given tighter financial conditions, downside risks to economic growth and the lack of material second-round effects from higher energy prices. The minutes reinforce expectations of a December rate hike, with policymakers indicating that further tightening would likely be necessary unless the inflation outlook improves significantly. The euro traded around 1.0986, up 0.10% on the day.

 SubjectiveContinuum Economics — ECB December Hike a Done Deal — Minutes ShowThe ECB released minutes to its October meeting in which policy rates were kept unchanged. The detail showed that a ‘large number’ of members had already been in favour of a rate hike at that meeting, and that, unless the inflation outlook improved significantly, ‘the only issue was timing’. A 2.50% deposit rate still sat within ECB staff estimates of the neutral rate, so it was not restraining the economy so much. A December hike looks almost like a done deal; the market is currently pricing in a 93% chance of a hike on 17 December.

 SubjectiveReuters, carried by 102.7 Super Hits — Thanksgiving storm knocks out power, disrupts flights on US East CoastA powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the US East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power for hundreds of thousands of users as wind gusts of up to 70 mph (112 kph) toppled trees and power lines. FlightAware reported a total of 417 US-related cancellations on Thursday and some 1,800 delayed by Thursday afternoon. More than 836,000 US utility customers had no power as of 4:06 p.m. ET (2106 GMT), including more than 174,000 in Virginia, 172,000 in Maryland and almost 170,000 in Pennsylvania, according to poweroutage.us; its data also showed more than 117,000 outages in Missouri, over 91,000 in New Jersey, more than 20,000 in Delaware and nearly 16,000 in North Carolina. New York City Emergency Management reported winds intensified on Thursday afternoon, reaching 56 mph (90 kph) at LaGuardia Airport. The threat of storms had already led officials to postpone Thursday’s 100th edition of the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.

 SubjectiveThe Wall Street Journal — Powerful Storm Hits East Coast, Scrambling Thanksgiving PlansA major storm is scrambling Thanksgiving Day plans along the East Coast, with heavy winds and rain causing power outages, flight cancellations and the postponement of Macy’s annual holiday parade. The National Weather Service said widespread coastal flooding was under way along the mid-Atlantic and New England coastline, with ‘significant inundation’ in Virginia, the Delaware Bay and parts of the Chesapeake Bay and southern New Jersey coast. Forecasters warned to expect flooded structures and impassable roads, as well as wind gusts of up to 60 mph along the coast and 50 mph further inland. Roughly 1,600 flights within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed, and more than 400 have been canceled, according to FlightAware; the hardest-hit airport thus far is Washington Dulles International Airport. As of early Thursday afternoon, more than 550,000 people were without power along the East Coast and mid-Atlantic, according to Poweroutage.us; the outages were concentrated in Maryland and Virginia, where Dominion said broken utility poles and large trees on power lines meant it could be days before power was restored in some areas. Another 123,000 power outages were reported in Missouri after several inches of snow fell on the eastern side of the state.

 SubjectiveCNN — Houthis strike Saudi oil infrastructure as Riyadh intensifies attacks on YemenA projectile struck an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s southwestern Jazan region on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several others, according to the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The strike sparked a fire and temporarily suspended some operations at the facility, the ministry said. A shipping source told CNN Thursday that oil loadings at the Ras Tanura terminal were suspended after the attack; it’s unclear whether they have resumed. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes ‘were accurate and direct’ and caused a fire at the Ras Tanura facility. The Saudi-led coalition said Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura, with falling debris but no injuries. In a statement Thursday, the coalition said it carried out a ‘precision military operation’ against Houthi capabilities, destroying 50 targets across Sanaa, Hodeidah and Saada governorates. The Houthi-controlled armed forces said Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 109 strikes over the previous 24 hours across Yemen, and the Houthi-controlled health ministry in Sanaa said at least 19 civilians had been killed and 25 others wounded in Saudi strikes over the previous 48 hours. CNN has approached Saudi state-owned oil giant Aramco for comment.

 SubjectiveReuters — Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say two oil tankers hit sea mines near Oman’s KhasabIran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman’s Khasab port while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorised route. Iran has long said that vessels cannot safely transit the Strait of Hormuz without coordinating with Tehran, citing the threat of sea mines among other risks.  SubjectiveStockBiz, carrying the wire from Hanoi — Trade partners react collectively to US proposal for new tariffsA number of economies, from the European Union and Japan to India and Singapore, have voiced opposition or expressed concern over the United States proposal to impose new tariffs, saying allegations of structural excess capacity are unfounded. European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill said on November 25 that the European Union strongly rejected the basis for the new tariff proposal, while stressing that the bloc was not a source of structural excess capacity, and that Brussels expects Washington to fully comply with the trade agreement reached in 2025, under which tariffs on European goods are capped at 15 percent. On November 26, Japan described the proposal as regrettable and rejected allegations of non-market trade practices or structural excess capacity. Singapore also expressed deep disappointment and disagreed with the findings of the Trade Representative’s office. Indonesia is reviewing the new import tariffs of up to 18 percent proposed on its goods. Under the proposal, Vietnam faces 35 percent, potentially falling to 20 percent if an agreement is reached. The measures are expected to be implemented only after a public hearing on January 25, 2027.

 SubjectiveDaily Inference — 14 economies, China and EU among them, face proposed US tariffsWashington has proposed tariffs on goods from 14 economies, including China and the European Union. A proposed 20 percent rate applies for many Chinese goods, with the possibility of a higher rate if negotiations fail. For the European Union, South Korea and Japan, a 15 percent rate is reported, in line with arrangements negotiated in recent months. Switzerland’s business association rejected Washington’s argument and said Switzerland’s surplus with the United States was driven primarily by pharmaceuticals and gold; the Swiss government said it expected any new tariffs to remain consistent with its framework deal. No retaliatory measures in response to this proposal have been announced so far.
